name: Section 25
label: Factory Records
lede: Ian Curtis produced their first single, Peter Saville wrapped their first album in waxed card, and Bernard Sumner helped them make "Looking from a Hilltop," the Blackpool electro record that New York clubs picked up.

eras.title: A sculptor comes home to Blackpool
eras.text: Larry Cassidy came back from art school with a first in sculpture and a bass guitar, and named his band after a clause in the Mental Health Act. A charity gig the Cassidy brothers put on in Blackpool got them in front of Joy Division, and Joy Division's singer ended up producing their first single.

years.src: LTM Recordings: Section 25 · Wikipedia: Larry Cassidy · Wikipedia: Section 25
years.h: The Cassidy brothers name their band after a detention order
years.p: [[Larry Cassidy|0b8e3895-6fda-41a9-9670-65b52aa1ffc2]] on bass and vocals, younger brother [[Vin Cassidy|47fe7137-a848-4429-8116-ed782d303c20]] on drums. Section 25 is the Mental Health Act clause that allows compulsory detention.
years.xp: Larry, born in 1953 into the Blackpool family that owned Casdon Toys, had skipped the family business to study sculpture at Maidstone College of Art, finishing in 1977. LTM's history dates the band to April 1978; Wikipedia says November 1977.

years.h: First gig: Lancaster City Football Club
years.p: Phil Denton, a civil servant, plays guitar. In November [[Paul Wiggin|f9d2cd89-6592-41a6-b7a3-aa79710b8657]] replaces him, and the trio that will make the Factory records is set.

years.h: The Cassidys put Joy Division and OMD on in Blackpool
years.p: A charity show for the International Year of the Child at the Imperial Hotel. [[Ian Curtis|10ae1bf6-88b2-4fb4-8fbe-8227a49803d3]] and manager [[Rob Gretton|41b55fab-da3b-4ecf-a67d-aeeec338a9c5]] like what they hear and push the band to record.

years.h: Ian Curtis brings Stephen Morris's Syndrum to Cargo Studios
years.p: Curtis and Gretton produce the session in Rochdale and pick three songs for Factory.
years.xp: "Ian and Rob gave us a lot of encouragement. They said they would come down and help us out with it," Vin Cassidy told LTM.

eras.title: Marble sleeves and a fear of flying
eras.text: The single came out two months after Curtis's death, the album came in one of the most expensive sleeves Peter Saville ever made for Factory, and the original trio ended over a flight to Helsinki.

years.h: FAC 18: "Girls Don't Count," produced by Ian Curtis and Rob Gretton
years.p: Recorded the previous September, it comes out two months after Curtis's death. The December 12-inch comes in three sleeves, each showing a woman from the band's circle.
years.xp: The three faces were Angela Cassidy, Larry and Vin's sister; Jenny Ross; and Julie Waddington. Earlier in 1980 the band had made its vinyl debut with "After Image," produced by [[Martin Hannett|ffbfce58-5185-4bcc-8c45-a7cd5d1a3783]], on the compilation Hicks from the Sticks. The NME's Kevin Fitzgerald: "Section 25 appear to have some idea of what they're doing."

years.h: Always Now comes in a waxed card pochette from Rouen
years.p: Hannett produces at Britannia Row in London and joins in on synth. [[Peter Saville|e61408b0-767c-4dde-ad88-a052456efcfe]]'s marbled sleeve costs a fortune; the first 10,000 copies sell quickly anyway.
years.xp: "Martin was really into the idea so he joined in and played some synth," Vin told LTM. On the packaging: "We were inexperienced about how much covers can actually cost a band."

years.h: Paul Wiggin won't fly to Helsinki, and the trio ends
years.p: The show is a [[New Order|f1106b17-dcbb-45f6-b938-199ccfab50cc]] support. Tony Wilson tries to recruit a teenage [[Johnny Marr|ff621094-2a76-401f-8398-b75b5fd2be24]] to replace Wiggin, without luck.
years.xp: LTM's history adds that Wiggin had already spent much of the fee getting there overland.

eras.title: Two drummers and a tape machine
eras.text: The brothers toured on backing tapes, got fed up with the heavy, moody material, and bought synthesizers with money from promoting a New Order show. With Larry's wife Jenny Ross and Bernard Sumner producing, they made a dance record that crossed onto Chicago R&B radio.

years.h: The 9:30 Club sees "a new kind of power trio"
years.p: First American tour, East Coast only: two Cassidys, percussionist [[Lee Shallcross|1aa235e3-c078-4619-9576-98f5ee9cd430]] and pre-recorded tapes. A Washington review supplies the line.
years.xp: A January European run with [[Crispy Ambulance|3420e6bc-8551-4c6c-86ca-c13a3115edd3]] used tapes too; percussionist John Grice had a panic attack after two shows and Crispy Ambulance's Gary Madeley took over.

years.h: The Key of Dreams includes a 15-minute "Sutra"
years.p: Self-made in their warehouse rehearsal space on Singleton Street, from more than five hours of tape. Factory Benelux puts it out.

years.h: Jenny Ross joins, and New Order money buys the synths
years.p: Larry's wife comes in on keyboards and vocals. The Roland gear is paid for with profits from promoting New Order's August show in Blackpool.
years.xp: "We didn't enjoy playing all that heavy moody stuff any more," Vin told LTM. "We just got fed up."

q: It's contemporary dance music. Soul music.
years.src: LTM Recordings: Section 25 · Wikipedia: From the Hip
years.h: Bernard Sumner produces From the Hip at Rockfield
years.p: Recorded in Wales in August 1983. Saville and Trevor Key lay coloured surveying poles up a hillside in Snowdonia for the cover.
years.xp: The album was licensed to eight territories. [[Bernard Sumner|6fa2e161-200e-475a-8492-3755594581f9]] said later that it showed him "just how much time and energy it takes to work on someone else's record."

years.src: LTM Recordings: Section 25 · Wikipedia: From the Hip
years.h: "Looking from a Hilltop" becomes a New York club record
years.p: Sumner and [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]]'s [[Donald Johnson|49569ee1-aba3-4c08-8ead-9791a7f8c96d]] rebuild it as FAC 108, in Restructure and Megamix versions. It crosses onto Chicago R&B stations; [[Orbital|f3e2a7d9-c6bb-4848-95e5-04c0a1e2f511]] and the Shamen later sample it.
years.xp: From May the band played as a five-piece with the Cassidys' sister Angela, as [[Angela Flowers|b4e87445-2e8c-42ba-b6cb-91309deeacd2]]. The New Yorker's Sasha Frere-Jones saw them at Danceteria and recalled he "couldn't get their weird sound out of my head."

years.h: Sixteen American dates and an ice-covered freeway
years.p: Boston to the Ritz in New York. Outside Chicago the hire car spins out of control.
years.xp:
Vin called it "a near-death experience." On the same tour Larry ran out of clean laundry and wore his trousers inside out, Vin told LTM; the lining was light pink, with the brand name, Hardcore, all over the legs.

Larry wasn't happy with Factory's push: "We've never had someone directly pushing us and shouting for us like the other big Factory bands have."

years.h: Vin Cassidy quits to support his family
years.p: Lee Shallcross goes hours later and Angela Flowers in February 1986. Larry and Jenny carry on.

eras.title: Bad news for "Bad News Week"
eras.text: Larry and Jenny finished a fourth album in 1986 and waited two years for it, held up first by Factory and then by a Factory press release.

years.big: An original song. 100% of the publishing to Jonathan King's company.
years.h: Factory's press office calls "Bad News Week" a Jonathan King cover
years.p: It wasn't one. King's publishers wanted a settlement, the band signed the publishing over to Jonjo Music, and copies were recalled. Love & Hate, finished in May 1986, finally comes out as FACT 160.
years.xp: Factory had already sat on the album, saying it took the tracks for demos. Bernard Sumner remixed "Bad News Week" at Yello 2 that September. The claim was that it covered King's 1965 "Good News Week."

eras.title: Back to Blackpool, then a new voice
eras.text: Factory's collapse and LTM's reissues brought the band back. They lost Jenny before they played a note live, gigged anyway, and brought in her and Larry's daughter Beth to sing.

years.h: Jenny Ross dies of cancer at 42
years.p: The band had regrouped in 2001 with Larry, Vin and Jenny. LTM's So Far DVD, out in January 2005, is dedicated to her.

years.h: Section 25 plays the Winter Gardens, Blackpool, with New Order
years.p: The first gigs in nearly two decades started in May in Poulton-le-Fylde, with Ian Butterworth of Tunnelvision on guitar.

years.h: Beth Cassidy sings on Nature + Degree
years.p: Larry and Jenny's daughter joins on vocals and keyboards. In December she and Larry share the mic at a Factory night in Brussels, with [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]] on the bill.

years.src: Wikipedia: Section 25 · LTM Recordings: Section 25 · Slicing Up Eyeballs
years.h: Larry Cassidy dies at home in Blackpool, aged 56
years.p: The cause was given as heart failure brought on by a blood clot. Members of [[New Order|f1106b17-dcbb-45f6-b938-199ccfab50cc]] and A Certain Ratio came to his funeral in Poulton-le-Fylde.
years.xp: "My brother Larry wasn't always the easiest person to be in a band with, but he was the best," Vin said.

years.h: Retrofit comes with Larry reading Joy Division's words
years.p: Finished after his death, with [[Stephen Morris|b3036249-8b39-4d02-a312-d31a63497bbc]] remaking "Looking from a Hilltop." Limited copies add a CD of Larry reading Joy Division lyrics, recorded in January 2010 on his last studio visit.

eras.title: Vin keeps the name
eras.text: Vin Cassidy has kept Section 25 going with Stephen Stringer. Old friends drop in, Simon Topping of A Certain Ratio among them on 2015's "Mirror," and the records keep coming: Duette, two albums "from the Bardo" and Move On in 2024.

years.h: Two years after Kanye sampled them, Elektra covers "FML"
years.p: Kanye West had used the Always Now track "Hit" on "FML" from The Life of Pablo in 2016. Elektra answers with an acoustic cover, original guitarist Paul Wiggin plays, and Michael Cassidy is on bass.
